title: Loop shaping with lead, lag, and PI

sections.body_md:
Loop shaping edits the loop transfer \(L(j\omega)\) until three things sit where you want them: the frequency where \(|L|\) crosses 1, the phase margin at that crossing, and the gain at low frequency. The blocks are ordinary. A lead adds phase in a band around one frequency. A lag, or a proportional-integral term, buys low-frequency gain relative to the gain at crossover. The plant itself is not rewritten.

You are drawing \(L\), not naming each closed-loop pole. The closed-loop behavior follows once the crossover and the margins are right, and it follows badly when a right-half-plane zero or a delay spends phase you cannot buy back.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For a lead with ratio \(\alpha > 1\), zero at \(-z\) and pole at \(-\alpha z\),
\[
\sin\phi_m = \frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + 1}, \qquad \omega_m = \sqrt{\alpha}\, z = \sqrt{|z|\,|p|}.
\]
The sine formula is the peak phase, not the phase at every frequency. A lag \((\tau s + 1)/(\beta \tau s + 1)\) with \(\beta > 1\) has high-frequency gain \(1/\beta\). A PI factor \(K_p(s + 1/\tau_i)/s\) has a pole at the origin and a zero you place below crossover.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(\alpha = 7\). Then \((\alpha-1)/(\alpha+1) = 0.75\), and \(\arcsin(0.75)\) is about 48.59 degrees of peak lead. Put the zero at \(1.6\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and the pole at \(11.2\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The bump is centered at \(\sqrt{1.6 \cdot 11.2} \approx 4.23\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). Set the gain so \(|L|\) is 1 at that center, then read the phase there again. If the low-frequency gain is still shy of the spec, add a lag whose upper corner is well below \(4.23\ \mathrm{rad/s}\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Swapping the corners turns a lead into a lag and spends phase instead of buying it. The peak formula returns a sine; treating \((\alpha-1)/(\alpha+1)\) as a number of degrees understates a modest lead and overstates a strong one. Centering the bump a decade away from the real crossover delivers almost none of \(\phi_m\) where it counts. And the lead's magnitude moves the crossing, so a margin computed on the bare plant is stale the moment you turn the gain.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A loop can be shaped only inside the limits set by right-half-plane zeros, unstable poles, and delay. Those bounds say how high the crossover can sit before the phase budget is gone. Shaping past that bound does not fail because the lead formula was wrong. It fails because no stable proper compensator can buy the phase back.
